item.title: ‘Just taking part was a victory’: veterans’ sport helps recovery in Ukraine
item.description:
Photographer David Levene meets service personnel and veterans at selection trials in Lviv for next year’s Invictus Games in Birmingham

It took a little longer than expected for the 100 or so archers to begin competing inside the large Soviet-era velodrome arena at MoD SKA in Lviv (built for the 1980 Moscow Olympics, it is Ukraine’s only indoor cycling track) on the first day of trials for the team that Ukraine will send to next year’s Invictus Games in Birmingham. The delay gave competitors a little extra time to stretch and practise. Coaches paraded up and down the line, giving some last-minute advice on strategy and technique to the waiting men and women facing down their targets.

Pavlo and Vadym share a laugh during the laser tag trials. Pavlo lost his left leg from a landmine in 2023 and swimming became his path to physical and mental recovery. Vadym suffered a frontline injury in 2022. He set a Ukrainian record for runners with below-knee amputations, completing the 42km Marine Corps Marathon in 3hrs 30m in October 2026.

item.title: UK to invest £9.5m in Ukraine windfarm to bolster war-hit energy system
item.description:
Project capable of powering 300,000 homes, with Britain having offered more than £770m to rebuild energy sector

Britain will add to its multimillion pound investments in rebuilding Ukraine’s energy system by funding a windfarm project capable of powering 300,000 Ukrainian households.

Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, said Britain would invest £9.5m to build a 200 megawatt windfarm in an undisclosed location to bolster Ukraine’s energy reserves as its war with Russia approaches the five-year mark.

item.title: The Danish prime minister’s coarse language about migrants has no place in the EU | Shada Islam
item.description:
Mette Frederiksen’s ‘great replacement’ remarks shows how centrist EU leaders have normalised previously shocking ideas

With the notable exception of Spain’s Pedro Sánchez, who may soon be out of office, EU leaders appear most united when promoting one clear aim: reinforcing the already heavily guarded borders of Fortress Europe against unwanted migrants.

Policymakers who once criticised Donald Trump’s immigration policies as inhumane now enact measures that increasingly resemble Washington’s ugly playbook of ICE home raids, family separations, deportations and offshore detention deals.

Shada Islam is a Brussels-based commentator on EU affairs. She runs New Horizons project, a strategy, analysis and advisory company
